title: Sounding natural
goal: React like a local, use tag questions and emphasis particles, make echo words, ask people to repeat or explain, get round words you don't know, and mix in English the way people do.
intro:
You can now say almost anything — this unit is about saying it the way people actually do. Real Hindi conversation is full of small words that textbooks skip: **ना** at the end of a sentence, **ही** and **तो** for emphasis, reactions like **हाय!**, **उफ़!**, **सच्ची?**, and echo words like **चाय-वाय** 'tea or something'.

You'll also learn the survival skills of a confident learner: stopping someone politely (**एक मिनट, क्या कहा?**), describing a word you've forgotten (**वो क्या कहते हैं…**) and mixing in English the way urban speakers do — *actually, basically, seriously*.

grammar.title: Tag questions: है ना?, ना, नहीं?
grammar.body:
English has dozens of tags (*isn't it? aren't you? didn't she?*). Hindi has essentially **one**: **ना** (also written **न**) at the end of the sentence.

**Checking / seeking agreement** — statement + **ना?** or **है ना?**:
आज बहुत गर्मी है, **है ना?** 'it's really hot today, isn't it?'
तुम कल आओगे **ना?** 'you'll come tomorrow, won't you?'
मज़ा आया **ना?** 'that was fun, wasn't it?'
**है ना** works after almost any sentence, whatever its own verb; plain **ना** attaches straight to the verb.

**Coaxing / softening a request** — imperative + **ना**:
बताओ **ना!** 'come on, tell me!' · चलो **ना** 'oh come on, let's go' · बैठिए **ना** 'please, do sit'
This makes a request warmer and more insistent, not ruder.

**Other tags** you'll hear: **ठीक है?** 'OK?', **सही?** 'right?', and **…, नहीं?** 'or not?' (तुम भी चलोगे, **नहीं?**).

**Intonation** does the work: a rising **ना?** asks; a falling, drawn-out **ना…** pleads.

The trap: **ना** at the end is a tag, **नहीं** before the verb is negation. तुम आओगे **ना**? 'you'll come, right?' vs तुम **नहीं** आओगे? 'you won't come?'

grammar.title: Emphasis: ही, तो, भी, भला
grammar.body:
Hindi stresses a word by putting a small **particle right after it**. Moving the particle changes the meaning.

**ही — only / exactly / the very**
मैं **ही** गया था 'only I went / it was me who went' · मैं गया **ही** नहीं 'I didn't go at all'
कल **ही** 'just yesterday / tomorrow itself' · आज **ही** 'today itself'
ही fuses with some words: यह + ही = **यही** 'this very', वह + ही = **वही** 'that very, the same', यहाँ + ही = **यहीं** 'right here', अब + ही = **अभी** 'right now', तब + ही = **तभी** 'just then', उस + ही = **उसी**.

**तो — as for / at least / contrast**
मैं **तो** जा रहा हूँ 'well, *I'm* going (whatever you do)' · तुम **तो** कमाल हो! 'you really are amazing!'
After a command, तो makes it gentle: देखो **तो** 'just have a look'.

**भी — also / even**
एक **भी** नहीं 'not even one' · कभी **भी** 'any time at all' · कुछ **भी** 'anything at all'

**भला — rhetorical 'why on earth'**
**भला** मैं क्यों जाऊँ? 'why on earth would I go?' It goes at the start of the question.

The trap: ही means 'only, exactly', **not** 'also' — मैं **ही** आया (only I came) vs मैं **भी** आया (I came too).

grammar.title: Echo words and doubled words: चाय-वाय, धीरे-धीरे
grammar.body:
**Echo words** are one of the most typical features of spoken Hindi (and of most South Asian languages). Repeat a word, replacing its first sound with **व** (or adding व before a vowel): the echo means '**… and that sort of thing**', '… or something':

चाय → **चाय-वाय** 'tea or something' · खाना → **खाना-वाना** 'food and stuff' · पैसे → **पैसे-वैसे** 'money and all that' · डॉक्टर → **डॉक्टर-वॉक्टर**
If the word already starts with व, people use another sound: वकील → **वकील-शकील**.

The echo is friendly and casual (चाय-वाय पियोगे?), or **dismissive** with a negative: मुझे डॉक्टर-वॉक्टर की ज़रूरत नहीं 'I don't need any doctor or whatever'.

**Doubled words** do different jobs:
**Distributive / 'all the…'** — **कौन-कौन** आ रहा है? 'who all is coming?' · **क्या-क्या** लाना है? 'what all do we need?'
**Gradual / repeated** — **धीरे-धीरे** 'slowly, little by little' · **कभी-कभी** 'sometimes' · **बार-बार** 'again and again'
**Variety** — **अलग-अलग** 'various, different' · **बड़े-बड़े** 'big ones'

Pairs of related words also go together: **थोड़ा-बहुत** 'a bit', **आस-पास** 'around', **घूमना-फिरना** 'going around'.

The trap: don't echo in formal situations (an interview, an email to your boss) — it sounds chatty.

dialogue.setting: Emma has lived in Delhi for a year. She meets her friend Rohit at a café in Hauz Khas.

lines.en: Ha ha, basically I learn from friends. Oh listen, yesterday I had that… what's it called… the round things with water inside…

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: हाँ, वही! और क़सम से, इतने तीखे थे कि आँखों से पानी आ गया।
lines.roman: hāṃ, vahī! aur qasam se, itne tīkhe the ki āṃkhoṃ se pānī ā gayā.
lines.en: Yes, those! And I swear, they were so spicy my eyes were streaming.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: फिर क्या, दस और खाए! पर रुको, तीखा और मसालेदार एक ही चीज़ है ना?

lines.en: Then what — I ate ten more! But wait, 'tikha' and 'masaledar' are the same thing, right?

lines.speaker: Rohit
lines.native: नहीं-नहीं। तीखा मतलब मिर्च वाला। मसालेदार मतलब बहुत सारे मसाले।
lines.roman: nahīṃ-nahīṃ. tīkhā matlab mirch vālā. masāledār matlab bahut sāre masāle.
lines.en: No, no. 'Tikha' means hot, with chilli. 'Masaledar' means lots of spices.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: एक मिनट, फिर से बोलना? आख़िरी वाली बात समझ में नहीं आई।
lines.roman: ek minaṭ, phir se bolnā? āxirī vālī bāt samajh meṃ nahīṃ āī.
lines.en: Hang on, say that again? I didn't get the last bit.

lines.speaker: Rohit
lines.native: मतलब, खाने में मसाले बहुत हों, तो भी ज़रूरी नहीं कि वो तीखा हो। समझी?
lines.roman: matlab, khāne meṃ masāle bahut hoṃ, to bhī zarūrī nahīṃ ki vo tīkhā ho. samjhī?
lines.en: I mean, food can have lots of spices and still not be hot. Got it?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: हम्म… समझ गई। चलो, आज मैं तुम्हें गोलगप्पे खिलाती हूँ — पैसे-वैसे की बात मत करना!
lines.roman: hmm… samajh gaī. chalo, āj maiṃ tumheṃ golgappe khilātī hūṃ — paise-vaise kī bāt mat karnā!
lines.en: Hmm… got it. Come on, today the golgappe are on me — don't even talk about money!

culture:
Urban Hindi is happily mixed with English — **Hinglish** — and a learner who says *actually*, *seriously* or *basically* in the middle of a Hindi sentence sounds more natural, not less. The grammar stays Hindi: *plan* **कैंसल कर दिया**, *bore* **हो गया**, *meeting* **में हूँ**. Formal Hindi (news, official letters) avoids this, but at a chai stall nobody speaks like the news.

The tone of a few small words carries a lot. **अच्छा** can mean 'OK', 'I see', 'really?' or 'oh, is that so' depending on how you say it; **हाँ जी** and **जी** on the phone show respect; **ना** makes a request warm. Slang varies by city: Delhi has **सच्ची**, **भाई**, **पका मत** 'don't bore me'; Mumbai has **झकास** 'awesome', **बिंदास** 'carefree', **भिड़ू** 'mate'. People are delighted when a foreigner speaks Hindi, and nobody minds you asking **X मतलब?** or **फिर से बोलना?** — it's how everyone keeps a conversation going.

tip.title: Reactions
tip.body:
- **वाह!** delight · **हाय!** sympathy ('oh no!') · **उफ़!** annoyance, heat · **छी!** disgust · **धत्!** 'damn!'
- **कमाल है!** / **ग़ज़ब!** — amazing (or outrageous).
- **अरे बाप रे!** — oh my God!
- Tone matters: the same word can be warm, shocked or sarcastic.

tip.title: है ना? — the one Hindi tag
tip.body:
- Statement + **है ना?** or **ना?** = isn't it? / won't you? / didn't she?: तुम कल आओगे **ना?**
- After a command, **ना** coaxes: बताओ **ना!** 'come on, tell me!'
- Don't mix it up with **नहीं** before the verb, which negates.

tip.title: ही, तो, भी — after the word they stress
tip.body:
- **ही** = only / exactly: मैं तो कल **ही** आया 'I only came yesterday'. यह + ही = **यही**, वह + ही = **वही**.
- **तो** = as for / really: तुम **तो** कमाल हो!
- **भी** = also / even: एक **भी** नहीं 'not even one'.
- **भला** starts a rhetorical question: **भला** मैं क्यों जाऊँ?

lessons.title: Tea or something: echo words

tip.title: चाय-वाय — echo words
tip.body:
- Repeat a word with **व** in place of its first sound: **चाय-वाय** 'tea or something', **पैसे-वैसे** 'money and all that'.
- Friendly and casual, or dismissive with a negative.
- Doubled words: **कौन-कौन** 'who all', **क्या-क्या** 'what all', **धीरे-धीरे** 'little by little'.

new: यह एक तरह की मिठाई है।

sentences.native: चलो, कहीं बाहर खाना-वाना खाते हैं।
sentences.roman: chalo, kahīṃ bāhar khānā-vānā khāte haiṃ.
sentences.en: Come on, let's go out and get some food or something.

sentences.native: मुझे डॉक्टर-वॉक्टर की ज़रूरत नहीं, बस आराम चाहिए।
sentences.roman: mujhe ḍokṭar-vokṭar kī zarūrat nahīṃ, bas ārām chāhiye.
sentences.en: I don't need a doctor or anything, I just need rest.

sentences.native: बाज़ार से क्या-क्या लाना है?
sentences.roman: bāzār se kyā-kyā lānā hai?
sentences.en: What all do we need from the market?

sentences.native: शादी में कौन-कौन आया था?
sentences.roman: shādī meṃ kaun-kaun āyā thā?
sentences.en: Who all came to the wedding?

sentences.native: पैसे-वैसे बाद में देख लेंगे।
sentences.roman: paise-vaise bād meṃ dekh leṃge.
sentences.en: We'll sort out the money and all that later.

sentences.native: मैं थोड़ा-बहुत पंजाबी भी समझ लेता हूँ।
sentences.roman: maiṃ thoṛā-bahut panjābī bhī samajh letā hūṃ.
sentences.en: I can understand a bit of Punjabi too.

sentences.native: हर तरह के लोग आए थे।
sentences.roman: har tarah ke log āye the.
sentences.en: All kinds of people came.

sentences.native: कभी-कभी मुझे भी ऐसा लगता है।
sentences.roman: kabhī-kabhī mujhe bhī aisā lagtā hai.
sentences.en: Sometimes I feel that way too.

lessons.title: Didn't catch that

tip.title: Keeping the conversation going
tip.body:
- Didn't catch it: **एक मिनट, क्या कहा?** · **फिर से बोलना?** · **समझ में नहीं आया**.
- Forgot the word? Describe it: **वो क्या कहते हैं…**, **एक तरह की …**, **ऐसी …-सी चीज़**.
- What does it mean? **X मतलब?** or **X का मतलब क्या होता है?**

new: बीच में टोकने के लिए सॉरी।

sentences.native: सॉरी, समझ में नहीं आया, थोड़ा धीरे बोलोगे?
sentences.roman: sorī, samajh meṃ nahīṃ āyā, thoṛā dhīre bologe?
sentences.en: Sorry, I didn't get that, could you speak a bit slower?

sentences.native: एक मिनट, तकल्लुफ़ मतलब क्या?
sentences.roman: ek minaṭ, takalluf matlab kyā?
sentences.en: Hang on, what does 'takalluf' mean?

sentences.native: वो क्या कहते हैं… हाँ, रसीद! रसीद चाहिए।
sentences.roman: vo kyā kahte haiṃ… hāṃ, rasīd! rasīd chāhiye.
sentences.en: What's the word… yes, receipt! I need a receipt.

sentences.native: मुझे इसका हिंदी नाम नहीं पता, बस ऐसी गोल-सी चीज़ है।
sentences.roman: mujhe iskā hindī nām nahīṃ patā, bas aisī gol-sī chīz hai.
sentences.en: I don't know what it's called in Hindi, it's this sort of roundish thing.

sentences.native: मुझे मत टोको, पहले पूरी बात सुनो।
sentences.roman: mujhe mat ṭoko, pahle pūrī bāt suno.
sentences.en: Don't interrupt me, hear me out first.

sentences.native: उसका लहजा बिल्कुल दिल्ली वालों जैसा है।
sentences.roman: uskā lahjā bilkul Dillī vāloṃ jaisā hai.
sentences.en: Her accent is just like a Delhiite's.

sentences.native: तुम्हारा लहजा तो बिल्कुल यहीं का लगता है!
sentences.roman: tumhārā lahjā to bilkul yahīṃ kā lagtā hai!
sentences.en: Your accent sounds totally local!

sentences.native: बीच में टोकना अच्छी बात नहीं है।
sentences.roman: bīch meṃ ṭoknā achchhī bāt nahīṃ hai.
sentences.en: It's not nice to interrupt.

tip.title: Hinglish the way people speak it
tip.body:
- Urban Hindi mixes in English freely: **एक्चुअली, बेसिकली, सीरियसली**.
- English words keep Hindi grammar: मीटिंग **में**, बोर **हो गया**, प्लान कैंसल **कर दिया**.
- English verbs come in with **करना / होना**: मिस **करना**, कॉल **करना**.
- In formal Hindi (news, letters) people mix much less.

sentences.native: एक्चुअली, मैं आज नहीं आ पाऊँगा।
sentences.roman: ekchualī, maiṃ āj nahīṃ ā pāūṃgā.
sentences.en: Actually, I won't be able to come today.

sentences.native: सीरियसली? तुमने फिर से प्लान कैंसल कर दिया?
sentences.roman: sīriyaslī? tumne phir se plān kainsal kar diyā?
sentences.en: Seriously? You cancelled the plan again?

sentences.native: बेसिकली, हमें कल तक सब ख़त्म करना है।
sentences.roman: besikalī, hameṃ kal tak sab xatm karnā hai.
sentences.en: Basically, we have to finish everything by tomorrow.

sentences.native: हम लोग बोलचाल में बहुत अंग्रेज़ी मिलाते हैं।
sentences.roman: ham log bolchāl meṃ bahut aṅgrezī milāte haiṃ.
sentences.en: We mix a lot of English into everyday speech.

sentences.native: बोलचाल की हिंदी किताबों वाली हिंदी से अलग है।
sentences.roman: bolchāl kī hindī kitāboṃ vālī hindī se alag hai.
sentences.en: Spoken Hindi is different from textbook Hindi.

sentences.native: सीरियसली यार, मैं तुम्हें बहुत मिस कर रहा हूँ।
sentences.roman: sīriyaslī yār, maiṃ tumheṃ bahut mis kar rahā hūṃ.
sentences.en: Seriously, mate, I really miss you.

sentences.native: चाय में चीनी मत मिलाना।
sentences.roman: chāy meṃ chīnī mat milānā.
sentences.en: Don't put sugar in the tea.

sentences.native: मैं बोर हो रहा हूँ, बेसिकली करने को कुछ नहीं है।
sentences.roman: maiṃ bor ho rahā hūṃ, besikalī karne ko kuchh nahīṃ hai.
sentences.en: I'm bored, there's basically nothing to do.
